extracted.intended_audience: writers, poets, playwrights, and educated readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles for composing and judging heroic poetry, allegory/personification, dramatic representation, and social/scene depiction in prose and drama. Emphasizes credibility of principal action, appropriate use of personification, diction, unity, and social detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility of heroic poem's principal parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroick Poem ought to appear credible in its principal Parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When imaginary persons are introduced as principal Actors engaged in a Series of Adventures, they 'take too much upon them' and are improper for heroic poetry. The primary actions and agents of a heroic poem should retain a believable, credible quality; avoid making central agents wholly shadowy or allegorical so as to damage the poem's verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable use of short allegorical personifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Short Allegories (imaginary Persons) are beautiful and effective when just shewn in brief expressions rather than engaged in prolonged action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief personifications (e.g., 'the Hours brought him his Reward', 'Victory sat on the right Hand') as poetical phrases to convey particular circumstances in a pleasing manner. These are to be taken figuratively, not literally, and function as rhetorical flourishes rather than as characters involved in the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit extended allegory as principal actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended allegorical figures (like Sin and Death) may be exquisite in kind but are 'not agreeable to the Nature of an Heroick Poem' when they act as principal agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such personifications can be admired for their imaginative power but, if they form the primary actors in a series of adventures, they undermine the poem's requirements for credible principal parts. Treat long allegories cautiously in epic contexts; prefer shorter, suggestive personifications or relegate extended allegory to non-epic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: choose apt words and phrases for personified action
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should find 'apt Words and Phrases' to describe the Actions of imaginary Persons and personifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong, precise language is necessary to make personifications vivid and effective. Readers familiar with the language will be 'amazed' at apt diction; invest time in selecting vocabulary that fits the imagined agency and scale of the figure (e.g., Death forming a bridge over Chaos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory as rhetorical figure vs literal agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between personified figures used as rhetorical figures and those presented as literal agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used as short figures of speech, personifications convey ordinary thoughts entertainingly; when portrayed as literal agents acting in the world, they require plausibility and may be inappropriate for certain genres (notably heroic epic). Use the figure type appropriate to the poem's tone and genre expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization to evoke sympathy (example: Eve)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals that elicit compassion use concrete, affecting actions (tears that cease not flowing, tresses disorderd, falling at feet, embracing, plaintive speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show emotion through physical detail and speech—e.g., Eve's humble embrace of Adam's feet and her pleading speech renew reader sympathy. Present inner conflict and despair (proposals to live childless or seek death) with delicacy, and let moral counterpoints (Adam's disapproval) clarify the intended moral without heavy-handedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey moral nuance subtly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid didactic bluntness; represent moral choices and their comparative virtues delicately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the essay notes that 'The Resolution of dying to end our Miseries, does not shew such a degree of Magnanimity as a Resolution to bear them, and submit to the Dispensations of Providence.' Present both the character's temptation and the corrective moral view through characterization and contrast rather than explicit moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene-setting and props to produce festivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Festive scenes should be set out so 'the Objects all around the Company gladdened their Hearts' (flowers, gay lights, music, agreeable company).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory detail—chaplets of flowers, artificial falls of water, intervals of soft notes, cheerful looks—to create an atmosphere of mirth. Such material details animate social scenes and make the mood convincing to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of 'pleasant companion' and frolick
rubrics_metrics.description: True frolick is 'the Play of the Mind' consisting of 'various and unforced Sallies of Imagination' by a person who knows rule and decency and can descend agreeably from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize witty companions as knowing decorum and choosing to relax it with grace; avoid depicting 'mirth' that consists only in ill-bred, mischievous or forced antics where the person knowingly behaves improperly. Good comic behavior arises from natural wit, mimicry that doesn't debase, and the ability to contribute to collective pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimicry should preserve dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective mimicry 'does not debase the Person he represents; but which, taking from the Gravity of the Character, adds to the Agreeableness of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting or staging mimicry, ensure the target's dignity is not wholly destroyed—use subtle gestures and expressions to amuse without mean-spirited humiliation. This approach keeps the satire gentle and socially acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of time and place (dramatic justness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers of Plays have Unity of Time and Place to give a Justness to their Representation; companions likewise should 'confine their Action to the Place of Meeting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect dramatic unities to maintain plausibility and cohesion. For scenes of social interaction, avoid sprawling actions that would strain credulity or require implausible movement; keep the dramatic 'stage' focused to preserve the representation's justness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance and dress as social signal
rubrics_metrics.description: A man's Appearance falls within the Censure of every one that sees him; dress influences reception—'a Stranger of tolerable Sense dressd like a Gentleman, will be better received by those of Quality'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In characterization and social scenes, use clothing and manners as reliable markers of status and reception. The essay defends modest self-improvement of appearance (e.g., two plain suits a year) for access to higher company—portray characters' appearance decisions realistically and show their social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve and measured style to imply learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Among strangers, reserve and the measured use of 'Delicacy, Idiom, fine Images, Structure of Periods, Genius, Fire' with 'frugal and comely Gravity' maintain the figure of immense reading and depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narration and dialogue, let learned or accomplished characters display depth by restraint rather than ostentation. Use elegant, economical phrasing and let occasional fine images imply erudition instead of constant display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sonic/performative devices in theatre (cat-call)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cat-call is a dramatic instrument that 'very much Improves the Sound of Nonsense' and can function as an adjunct to actors or a substitute for chorus; it can also be trained to signify critical judgments (smut-note, fustian-note, Stupid-note, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting theatrical criticism or staging, consider how non-musical sound-effects and audience instruments can function rhetorically—accompanying actors, signaling disapproval, or amplifying comedic/tragic effect. Sound can be used deliberately to comment on violations (e.g., of the unities) or the quality of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound effects' psychological/performative power
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain sound mixtures (Collier's 'Anti-Musick') can 'sink the Spirits, and shake the Nerves' and in practice the cat-call has 'struck a Damp into Generals, and frighted Heroes off the Stage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dramatic composition and criticism, beware of and exploit the capacity of auditory elements to influence audience emotions and performers: judiciously used, non-musical noises can undermine or bolster a scene's effect; depict or design them with intention.
